title: Alliance Formation and Complexity of Indo‐Pacific Bottlenose Dolphins (Tursiops aduncus) Around Mikura Island, Japan
content:
ABSTRACT

In this study, we investigated alliance formation and complexity in male Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins around Mikura Island using 5 years of data collected through underwater observations. Focusing on 18 mature males, we examined affiliative behaviors (proximity and rubbing), consortships, and associations. First, we tested the relationship between association and behaviors and found that the probability of observing each behavior increased significantly with association frequency. This suggests that alliances are formed in this community. Second, to determine alliance membership for each individual, we evaluated a size-constrained model (small alliances) and a size-unconstrained model (a mixture of small and large alliances). In both models, candidate alliance units were determined by association, and the models were evaluated by the extent to which affiliative behaviors and consortship were concentrated within units. All three behaviors were more concentrated within units under the size-unconstrained model than under the size-constrained model, so the former was further investigated. Given the observed variation in alliance size and within-alliance relationships, as well as the fact that only a few males cooperate in a single consortship, we suggest that alliance complexity in the Mikura community shares some similarities with that in the Shark Bay community, where males form complex, multi-level alliances.
